NowEDA Playground — 0.2.2¶

Run this notebook from the repository root with NowEDA and noweda[viz] installed in the selected kernel. Restart the kernel after changing the package source.

  1. Core workflow — read, assess, visualize, choose an ML direction, investigate, compare, and report
  2. Advanced tables — focused quality, relationship, privacy, and encoding evidence
  3. Advanced extensions — custom plugin workflows and chunked reading

The loading indicator shows elapsed time while work is running. 100% means the operation completed; an explicitly closed stream shows Stopped before completion if you did not consume it fully. It does not estimate rows read.

Setup¶

In [1]:
from pathlib import Path
from contextlib import closing
import noweda as eda
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None)
pd.set_option('display.max_columns', None)

Load Your Data¶

The repository includes a 100,000-row, 32-column synthetic CSV with identifiers, PII-like values, missingness, dates, rare categories, outliers, duplicates, correlated features, Base64 text, and supervised ML targets. No real personal data is used. Change FILE for another dataset. The main examples use small mode on the first 10,000 rows to keep notebook execution quick. The next cell also shows explicit large mode: it keeps the full supported source on disk, reports exact dimensions, and labels bounded-sample findings before analysis.

In [2]:
FILE = Path('test_data_large_with_pii.csv')
if not FILE.is_file():
    raise FileNotFoundError('Run from the repository root, or set FILE to your CSV.')

# Small mode (default): returns a pandas DataFrame.
df = eda.read(FILE, nrows=10_000)
print(f'Small mode preview: {len(df):,} rows x {len(df.columns)} columns')

# Large mode: keeps the source on disk. Use an integer, not a quoted string,
# for chunksize. Its supported .eda methods announce sample-based findings.
# statsall(), vizall(), and mlall() default to sample=10_000 in large mode.
large_data = eda.read(FILE, mode='large', chunksize=10_000)
print(f'Large mode source: {large_data.shape[0]:,} rows x {large_data.shape[1]} columns')
large_report = large_data.eda.report()
print(f"Large-mode scope: {large_report['large_mode']['result_scope']}")
print('Large-mode preview (read from disk):')
print(large_data.head())

# Large mode defaults to a 10,000-row analysis sample. Adjust per method:
# large_data.eda.statsall()                 # sample=10_000 by default
# large_data.eda.vizall(target='fraud_flag', sample=5_000, max_plots=10)
# large_data.eda.mlall(target='fraud_flag', sample=25_000)
df.head()

SECTION 1: The 5 Powerful Methods (Primary Usage)¶

These methods do comprehensive analysis in a single call. Perfect for understanding your data end-to-end.

1. df.eda.statsall() — Complete Statistical Analysis¶

Prints a rich report with:

  • Data quality scores
  • Column types and inferred roles
  • Descriptive statistics (mean, std, quartiles, skewness)
  • Missing data summary
  • Duplicate detection
  • Outlier counts
  • Human-readable insights
  • ML preprocessing recommendations
In [3]:
# Small mode analyzes every row already loaded in `df` by default.
df.eda.statsall()

# Use a bounded sample only when you request one:
# df.eda.statsall(sample=5_000)

2. df.eda.vizall() — Explore visually¶

Use charts after the statistical assessment identifies areas worth exploring. Small mode uses every loaded row by default. Pass sample=10_000 (or another positive integer) to bound statsall(), vizall(), or mlall(). Large mode uses sample=10_000 by default; change it up or down per method.

What the charts cover¶

Without a target, NowEDA ranks general distributions, missingness, outliers, feature scales, associations, numeric relationships, and temporal patterns. max_plots limits individual panels rather than only top-level figures.

In [4]:
# Small mode: chart and supporting analysis use all loaded rows.

Add target-aware ML diagnostics¶

The user selects the prediction target. NowEDA infers classification or regression, ranks useful non-PII features, and shows evidence for linear and nonlinear model families. The charts guide what to validate; they do not declare a winning model.

In [5]:
target_visuals = df.eda.vizall(
    target="fraud_flag",
    max_plots=15,
)
target_visuals

[########################] 100% NowEDA · Rendering visualizations
Visual ML signals
  - Possible target leakage: fraud_risk_score has a near-deterministic univariate association; verify when it becomes available.
  - Choose between linear and nonlinear classifiers with stratified validation; visual separation alone is not decisive.
Out[5]:
NowEDA VizResult(target='fraud_flag', problem_type='classification', plots=15, selected_features=14)

3. df.eda.mlall() — Choose an ML direction¶

Start without arguments when the objective is unknown. Then name the outcome column for supervised guidance.

In [6]:
# Small mode uses all loaded rows unless `sample=` is supplied.
# Start with an objective-free assessment, then name the target you intend to predict.
df.eda.mlall()

classification_features = [
    'account_balance', 'transaction_count', 'account_age_days', 'region', 'satisfaction_score'
]

# Infer the supervised problem from the named target, print guidance, and inspect it.
classification_plan = df.eda.mlall(
    target='account_status',
    features=classification_features,
    plan=True,
)

# Example bounded ML guidance: df.eda.mlall(target='fraud_flag', sample=5_000)
print(
    classification_plan['problem_type'],
    classification_plan['problem_subtype'],
    '—',
    classification_plan['inference_reason'],
)

  Gradient-Boosted Trees
    Estimated fit: ★★★★★ (4.5/5)
    Why: Strong candidate for nonlinear tabular relationships and mixed feature types.
    Caution: Tune with validation data and early stopping; performance is not established by this recommendation.

  Logistic Regression
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (4.0/5)
    Why: Interpretable probability baseline for binary or multiclass outcomes.
    Caution: Encode categoricals, scale numeric features, and use regularization for correlated features.

  Random Forest Classifier
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (4.0/5)
    Why: Captures nonlinear interactions and provides a robust tree-based baseline.
    Caution: Impute missing values and validate depth to limit overfitting, especially on small data.

  Support Vector Classifier
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Can model complex boundaries on small or medium numeric datasets.
    Caution: Requires scaling and can become expensive as row count grows.

  Preprocessing
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    1. Encode categorical features inside the fitted pipeline; handle unseen categories.
    2. Scale numeric features for distance-, margin-, and component-based methods.
    3. Use class weights or resampling within training folds; never resample validation rows.

  Validation and metrics
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    • Use stratified holdout or cross-validation when every class has enough rows.
    • Compare macro F1, weighted F1, per-class recall, confusion matrix, and log loss.

Other supported ML objectives¶

The same API covers regression, clustering, anomaly detection, and dimensionality reduction. Unsupervised objectives omit target. The table below keeps the playground compact while executing every supported path.

In [7]:
numeric_features = ['transaction_count', 'account_age_days', 'satisfaction_score']

plans = {
    'regression': df.eda.mlall(
        target='account_balance',
        problem_type='regression',
        features=numeric_features,
        plan=True,
    ),
    'clustering': df.eda.mlall(
        problem_type='clustering',
        features=numeric_features,
        plan=True,
    ),
    'anomaly_detection': df.eda.mlall(
        problem_type='anomaly_detection',
        features=numeric_features,
        plan=True,
    ),
    'dimensionality_reduction': df.eda.mlall(
        problem_type='dimensionality_reduction',
        features=numeric_features,
        plan=True,
    ),
}

pd.DataFrame([
    {
        'objective': objective,
        'target': plan['target'],
        'first_candidate': plan['recommendations'][0]['name'],
        'candidate_count': len(plan['recommendations']),
    }
    for objective, plan in plans.items()
])

  --------------------------------------------------------------
    • Use holdout or K-fold validation; use grouped or time-aware splits when rows are dependent.

======================================================================

  Problem type: clustering

  Candidate methods (ranked by estimated fit)
  --------------------------------------------------------------

  K-Means or MiniBatchKMeans
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (4.0/5)
    Why: Fast centroid baseline for scaled numeric features.
    Caution: Assumes roughly compact clusters and requires choosing the number of clusters.

  DBSCAN
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Finds nonspherical dense groups and labels sparse observations as noise.
    Caution: Sensitive to scaling and neighborhood parameters; distance degrades in many dimensions.

  Agglomerative Clustering
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Exposes hierarchical group structure without centroid assumptions.
    Caution: Memory and runtime make it best suited to smaller datasets.

  Preprocessing
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    1. Scale numeric features for distance-, margin-, and component-based methods.
    2. Exclude identifiers and features unavailable at the point where the method will be used.

  Validation and metrics
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    • Compare silhouette and stability across seeds or resamples, then inspect cluster usefulness with domain experts.
    • Internal cluster scores do not prove that groups are meaningful for the intended decision.

  Guidance is based on data characteristics; no models were trained or measured.

======================================================================

  Problem type: anomaly_detection

  Candidate methods (ranked by estimated fit)
  --------------------------------------------------------------

  Isolation Forest
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (4.0/5)
    Why: Scales well and detects unusual multivariate combinations without labels.
    Caution: The contamination assumption changes the alert threshold and needs domain review.

  Local Outlier Factor
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Finds observations that are unusual relative to their local neighborhood.
    Caution: Scale features; scoring new unseen rows requires novelty mode.

  One-Class SVM
    Estimated fit: ★★★☆☆ (3.0/5)
    Why: Can learn nonlinear boundaries around typical observations on smaller datasets.
    Caution: Sensitive to scaling and hyperparameters and expensive as row count grows.

  Preprocessing
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    1. Scale numeric features for distance-, margin-, and component-based methods.
    2. Exclude identifiers and features unavailable at the point where the method will be used.

  Validation and metrics
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    • Review top-ranked anomalies and alert volume with domain experts; test stability across windows or samples.
    • If labels exist, use precision-recall metrics and cost at an operational threshold.

  Guidance is based on data characteristics; no models were trained or measured.

  Problem type: dimensionality_reduction

  Candidate methods (ranked by estimated fit)
  --------------------------------------------------------------

  PCA
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (4.0/5)
    Why: Reproducible linear compression for scaled dense numeric features.
    Caution: Components may be hard to interpret and cannot directly consume raw categoricals.

  Truncated SVD
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Works with sparse encoded matrices and avoids centering them.
    Caution: Like PCA, it captures linear structure and component meaning may be unclear.

  UMAP or t-SNE for exploration
    Estimated fit: ★★★★☆ (3.5/5)
    Why: Useful for visualizing possible nonlinear neighborhoods in two or three dimensions.
    Caution: Plots can change with parameters and random seeds; do not treat visual groups as validated clusters.

  Preprocessing
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    1. Scale numeric features for distance-, margin-, and component-based methods.
    2. Exclude identifiers and features unavailable at the point where the method will be used.

  Validation and metrics
  --------------------------------------------------------------
    • For PCA/SVD, inspect explained variance, reconstruction error, and downstream validation performance.
    • For visualization embeddings, test stability across parameters and random seeds.

  Guidance is based on data characteristics; no models were trained or measured.

Advanced: export JSON and HTML reports¶

Strict JSON maps undefined/nonfinite statistics to null. HTML includes score contributions and Base64 sample counts. This example uses a temporary directory.

In [21]:
from noweda.report.json import generate_json_report
from noweda.report.html import generate_html_report
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as output_dir:
    report = df.eda.report()
    generate_json_report(report, Path(output_dir) / "report.json")
    generate_html_report(report, Path(output_dir) / "report.html")
    print("Strict JSON and HTML reports generated successfully.")

[########################] 100% NowEDA · Building report
Strict JSON and HTML reports generated successfully.

SECTION 3: The Plugin System (Custom Analysis Workflows)¶

Run specific plugins for lightweight, custom analysis. Useful when you only care about certain checks.

How Plugins Work¶

Accessor reports combine the eight default plugins. You can also run plugins manually for:

  • Lightweight analysis (run only what you need)
  • Custom workflows (combine built-in + your own plugins)
  • Programmatic access to raw results

Available Plugins:

  • SchemaPlugin — Column roles & types
  • StatsPlugin — Descriptive statistics
  • MissingDataPlugin — Missing value rates
  • DuplicatesPlugin — Duplicate rows & constants
  • CorrelationPlugin — Correlation matrix
  • OutlierPlugin — Outlier counts
  • PIIDetectorPlugin — PII findings
  • EncodingDetectionPlugin — Encoding signals

Example 1: Quick Data Quality Check¶

Run only the plugins that matter for data quality: missing data, duplicates, outliers and statistics. Stats supply the observed-value denominator for outlier scoring. Scores from a partial plugin stack omit checks that were not run.

In [22]:
from noweda.core.engine import AutoEDAEngine
from noweda.plugins.missing import MissingDataPlugin
from noweda.plugins.duplicates import DuplicatesPlugin
from noweda.plugins.outliers import OutlierPlugin
from noweda.plugins.stats import StatsPlugin

# Create engine with only the plugins we need
engine = AutoEDAEngine([
    MissingDataPlugin(),
    DuplicatesPlugin(),
    OutlierPlugin(),
    StatsPlugin(),
])

# Run analysis
report = engine.run_df(df)

# Access results
print("=" * 70)
print("DATA QUALITY CHECK")
print("=" * 70)

print("\n📊 MISSING DATA:")
missing = report['results']['missing']
for col, rate in missing.items():
    if rate > 0:
        print(f"  {col}: {rate*100:.1f}% missing")
if all(rate == 0 for rate in missing.values()):
    print("  ✓ No missing data")

print("\n🔄 DUPLICATES & CONSTANTS:")
dups = report['results']['duplicates']
print(f"  Duplicate rows: {dups['duplicate_rows']}")
print(f"  Constant columns: {dups['constant_columns'] or 'None'}")

print("\n⚠️  OUTLIERS:")
outliers = report['results']['outliers']
for col, count in outliers.items():
    if count > 0:
        observed = df[col].count()
        pct = count / observed * 100 if observed else 0
        print(f"  {col}: {count} outliers ({pct:.1f}% of observed values)")
if all(count == 0 for count in outliers.values()):
    print("  ✓ No outliers detected")

Example 4: Write Your Own Custom Plugin¶

Create a custom plugin to add domain-specific analysis. This example distinguishes identifiers, temporal fields, and high-cardinality text instead of treating every unique value as an ID.

In [25]:
import pandas as pd

from noweda.plugins.base import BasePlugin

class HighCardinalityPlugin(BasePlugin):
    """Review highly unique fields without treating every one as an ID."""
    name = "high_cardinality"

    def run(self, df):
        results = {}
        for col in df.columns:
            unique_ratio = df[col].nunique() / len(df) if len(df) else 0
            if unique_ratio <= 0.95:
                continue

            name = str(col).lower()
            if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[col]):
                if name == 'id' or '_id' in name or name.startswith('id_'):
                    warning = 'Likely identifier — exclude from model features.'
                else:
                    continue  # Continuous numeric values are normally unique.
            else:
                sample = df[col].dropna().astype(str).head(20)
                parsed = pd.to_datetime(sample, errors='coerce', format='mixed')
                if not sample.empty and parsed.notna().mean() >= 0.8:
                    warning = 'Temporal field — parse as datetime and derive temporal features.'
                else:
                    warning = ('High-cardinality text — it may be an identifier, PII, or free text; '
                               'do not encode automatically.')

            results[col] = {'unique_ratio': unique_ratio, 'warning': warning}
        return results

# Use the custom plugin
custom_plugin = HighCardinalityPlugin()
engine = AutoEDAEngine([custom_plugin])
report = engine.run_df(df)

print("=" * 70)
print("HIGH-UNIQUENESS REVIEW (Custom Plugin)")
print("=" * 70)

results = report['results']['high_cardinality']
if results:
    for col, info in results.items():
        print(f"\n⚠️  {col}")
        print(f"   Unique ratio: {info['unique_ratio']:.1%}")
        print(f"   {info['warning']}")
else:
    print("\n✓ No high-uniqueness fields need review")

Example 5: Combine Built-in & Custom Plugins¶

Mix built-in plugins with your custom ones for a tailored workflow.

# Create engine with mix of built-in and custom
engine = AutoEDAEngine([
    SchemaPlugin(),
    MissingDataPlugin(),
    custom_plugin,  # Our custom plugin from above
])

report = engine.run_df(df)

print("=" * 70)
print("COMBINED ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 70)

# Show schema
print("\n📋 SCHEMA:")
for col, info in report['results']['schema'].items():
    print(f"  {col}: {info['role']}")

# Show missing data
print("\n📊 MISSING DATA:")
for col, rate in report['results']['missing'].items():
    if rate > 0:
        print(f"  {col}: {rate*100:.1f}%")

# Show high cardinality warnings
print("\n⚠️  HIGH CARDINALITY:")
if report['results']['high_cardinality']:
    for col in report['results']['high_cardinality'].keys():
        print(f"  {col}")
else:

Extended Example: New PII Patterns¶

NowEDA now detects four types of PII:

  • Email: Standard email format
  • Phone: Ten-digit US-style formats (including +1, dashes, spaces, parentheses)
  • SSN: Social Security Numbers (123-45-6789 or 123 45 6789)
  • Credit Card: Supported Visa, Mastercard, Amex and Discover patterns with Luhn validation; spaces and hyphens are accepted Counts represent matching cells per PII type. Pattern checks can miss sensitive values or flag false positives; zero findings do not establish safety.
In [27]:
# Create a dataset with multiple PII types
import pandas as pd

df_pii = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': ['CUST001', 'CUST002', 'CUST003', 'CUST004'],
    'email': ['alice@company.com', 'bob@example.org', 'charlie.brown@mail.com', 'diana@test.net'],
    'phone': ['(555) 123-4567', '+1-800-555-0100', '555.987.6543', '(212) 555-1234'],
    'ssn': ['123-45-6789', '987-65-4320', '555-12-3456', 'N/A'],
    'credit_card': ['4532 0151 1283 0366', '5425-2334-3010-9903', '378282246310005', 'XXXXXXXXXXXX'],
    'notes': ['Good customer', 'Call 555-1234 for follow-up', 'Email: test@test.com', 'No notes'],
})

print("DataFrame with multiple PII types:")
print(df_pii)

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("PII DETECTION RESULTS")
print("="*70)

pii_results = df_pii.eda.pii_df()
print(pii_results)

print("\nPII Summary:")
for pii_type in pii_results['PII_Type'].unique():
    count = pii_results[pii_results['PII_Type'] == pii_type]['Count'].sum()
    columns = pii_results[pii_results['PII_Type'] == pii_type]['Column'].tolist()
    print(f"  {pii_type.upper()}: {count} instances in columns {columns}")

Extended Example: Chunked Ingestion¶

CSV/JSON and all chunked reads use pandas. concat=True retains every chunk and allocates a combined DataFrame, so the full data and concatenation overhead must fit in RAM. concat=False lets you process chunks without retaining them all.

Use contextlib.closing() when iterating: it closes the file reader and loading indicator even if you break early or processing raises an exception. Fully consuming the stream produces the 100% completion indicator.

In [28]:
# Example 1: A small CSV that demonstrates chunk boundaries
import tempfile
import os

# Create a 100-row CSV (not a large-file benchmark)
tmp = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.csv', delete=False, mode='w')
tmp.write('id,name,value,status\n')
for i in range(100):
    tmp.write(f'{i},record_{i},{i*100},active\n')
tmp.close()

print(f"Created test file: {tmp.name}")
print(f"File size: {os.path.getsize(tmp.name)} bytes")

# Read in chunks, but get a single concatenated DataFrame
df_large = eda.read_chunked(tmp.name, chunksize=20)
print(f"\nLoaded DataFrame: {df_large.shape}")
print(df_large.head())

# Run analysis on the concatenated result
print("\nQuick stats:")
print(df_large.eda.scores_df())

In [29]:
# Example 2: Process pandas chunks one at a time
print("Processing file in chunks (concat=False):")
print("="*70)

chunk_count = 0
total_rows = 0
pii_findings_all = []

# Iterate through chunks
with closing(eda.read_chunked(tmp.name, chunksize=20, concat=False)) as chunks:
    for chunk in chunks:
        chunk_count += 1
        total_rows += len(chunk)
        
        print(f"\nChunk {chunk_count}: {chunk.shape}")
        print(f"  Columns: {list(chunk.columns)}")
        print(f"  First row: {chunk.iloc[0].to_dict()}")
        
        # Analyze this chunk
        chunk_pii = chunk.eda.pii_df()
        if len(chunk_pii) > 0:
            pii_findings_all.append(chunk_pii)

print(f"\n" + "="*70)
print(f"Processed {chunk_count} chunks, {total_rows} total rows")
print("Only per-chunk summaries are retained; chunks are not collected into a list.")

# Cleanup
os.unlink(tmp.name)
print("\n✓ Cleanup complete")

Advanced: Chunked Ingestion Techniques¶

The following cells use the complete CSV selected in FILE. DataFrame memory measurements below count stored column values; they do not measure process peak memory or include parser buffers, analysis results and other notebook variables.

In [30]:
import os
TEST_FILE = FILE
print(f'File size: {os.path.getsize(TEST_FILE) / (1024**2):.2f} MiB')

File size: 38.59 MiB

Technique 1: Load All Chunks, Return a Single DataFrame¶

For data that fits in RAM, including the chunks and concatenation overhead. Chunking followed by concatenation does not guarantee lower peak memory.

In [31]:
# Read in 10,000-row chunks and concatenate
print("Loading the full CSV in pandas chunks...")
df_chunked = eda.read_chunked(TEST_FILE, chunksize=10_000)

print(f"✓ Loaded {len(df_chunked):,} rows × {len(df_chunked.columns)} columns")
print(f"✓ Memory usage: {df_chunked.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / (1024**2):.2f} MB")
print(f"\nShape: {df_chunked.shape}")
print(f"Columns: {list(df_chunked.columns)}")
print(f"\nFirst row:")
print(df_chunked.iloc[0])
# Release this full-size result before the subsequent streaming examples.
del df_chunked

Technique 2: Stream Chunks One-at-a-Time¶

Best for: Files too large for RAM, or when you need to process/aggregate per-chunk.

In [32]:
# Process chunks without loading the entire file
print("Streaming chunks (concat=False):")
print("Pandas reads each chunk; only score summaries are retained.")
print("="*70)

chunk_metrics = []
total_rows = 0
chunk_count = 0
max_chunk_bytes = 0

with closing(eda.read_chunked(TEST_FILE, chunksize=25000, concat=False)) as chunks:
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks, 1):
        chunk_count += 1
        total_rows += len(chunk)
        max_chunk_bytes = max(max_chunk_bytes, chunk.memory_usage(deep=True).sum())
        
        # Run analysis on this chunk
        scores = chunk.eda.scores_df().T
        scores['chunk'] = i
        chunk_metrics.append(scores)
        
        print(f"Chunk {i}: {len(chunk):,} rows")
        print(f"  Data Quality: {scores['data_quality'].iloc[0]:.1f}")
        print(f"  Model Readiness: {scores['model_readiness'].iloc[0]:.1f}")
        print(f"  Risk Score: {scores['risk'].iloc[0]:.1f}")

print(f"\nTotal: {total_rows:,} rows processed in {chunk_count} chunks")
print(f"Largest chunk DataFrame: {max_chunk_bytes / (1024**2):.2f} MiB (not peak process memory)")
# These per-chunk scores are not whole-dataset scores.

Technique 3: PII Detection Across Large Dataset¶

Detect and collect PII from all chunks.

In [33]:
# Aggregate PII findings across all chunks
print("PII Detection Across Chunks:")
print("="*70)

pii_by_chunk = {}
all_pii = []

with closing(eda.read_chunked(TEST_FILE, chunksize=20000, concat=False)) as chunks:
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks, 1):
        chunk_pii = chunk.eda.pii_df()
        
        if len(chunk_pii) > 0:
            chunk_pii['chunk_num'] = i
            all_pii.append(chunk_pii)
            
            # Summary for this chunk
            total = chunk_pii['Count'].sum()
            pii_by_chunk[i] = total
            print(f"Chunk {i}: {total:,} PII instances")
        else:
            pii_by_chunk[i] = 0
            print(f"Chunk {i}: No PII detected")

# Combine all PII findings
if all_pii:
    combined_pii = pd.concat(all_pii, ignore_index=True)
    print(f"\nTotal PII instances found: {combined_pii['Count'].sum():,}")
    print(f"\nPII Breakdown:")
    summary = combined_pii.groupby('PII_Type')['Count'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
    print(summary)
else:
    print("No PII detected in any chunk")

Technique 4: Custom Delimiter (Pipe-Separated Values)¶

Forward sep parameter for non-standard delimiters.

In [34]:
# Example: If you had a pipe-delimited file
# df = eda.read_chunked('data.csv', chunksize=10_000, sep='|')

# For JSON files with newline-delimited records
# df = eda.read_chunked('data.jsonl', chunksize=10_000)

# TSV files (tab-separated) - detected automatically by extension
# df = eda.read_chunked('data.tsv', chunksize=10_000)

# With additional pandas parameters
# df = eda.read_chunked('data.csv', chunksize=10_000, dtype={'col1': 'int32'}, na_values=['NA', 'N/A'])

DataFrame Memory Comparison¶

Compare a full DataFrame with the largest individual chunk while consuming the whole file in every mode. Row totals must agree. These are measured DataFrame sizes, not peak process memory; the notebook may retain other objects and parser buffers. No fixed memory-saving percentage is assumed.

In [35]:
file_path = TEST_FILE
print(f'File on disk: {os.path.getsize(file_path) / (1024**2):.2f} MiB')

# 1. Load the complete CSV through NowEDA.
df_all = eda.read(file_path)
rows_all = len(df_all)
mem_all = df_all.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / (1024**2)
print(f'eda.read(): {rows_all:,} rows; DataFrame size {mem_all:.2f} MiB')
del df_all

# 2. Retain all chunks and concatenate into a complete DataFrame.
df_combined = eda.read_chunked(file_path, chunksize=10_000)
rows_combined = len(df_combined)
mem_combined = df_combined.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / (1024**2)
print(f'concat=True: {rows_combined:,} rows; DataFrame size {mem_combined:.2f} MiB')
del df_combined

# 3. Consume the ENTIRE stream, retaining only counters and the largest size.
rows_streamed = 0
chunk_count = 0
largest_chunk_bytes = 0
with closing(eda.read_chunked(file_path, chunksize=10_000, concat=False)) as chunks:
    for chunk in chunks:
        rows_streamed += len(chunk)
        chunk_count += 1
        largest_chunk_bytes = max(largest_chunk_bytes, chunk.memory_usage(deep=True).sum())
        del chunk

assert rows_streamed == rows_all == rows_combined
print(f'concat=False: completed {chunk_count} chunks; {rows_streamed:,} rows')
print(f'Largest chunk DataFrame: {largest_chunk_bytes / (1024**2):.2f} MiB')
print('All three modes read the same number of rows. These sizes are not peak memory measurements.')
